resources.string: Traits below are common clues, not a universal identification key. A family is a lineage; trees, herbs and food crops are descriptive collections that can contain unrelated lineages.
Differences and nested groups

Nested groups represented in this tree

Green plants include green algae and land plants. Land plants are one nested lineage, not a separate counterpart to all algae. Photosynthesis also occurs in unrelated organisms through different plastid histories.

Land plants retain and nourish a multicellular embryo. Mosses, liverworts and hornworts lack the vascular organization of ferns and seed plants; many species returned to water. Terrestrial habitat alone does not define membership.

Xylem and phloem transport water and organic substances. Lycophytes and ferns reproduce without seeds; seed plants share vascular tissues but add pollen and ovules. A spore is one cell, whereas a seed contains an embryo and reserves.
Gymnosperm ovules are not enclosed in an ovary; angiosperm ovules are. Gymnosperms therefore have seeds but no true fruits. Pollination carries pollen before fertilization; these are distinct events.

Angiosperms enclose ovules in carpels and form fruits. Double fertilization commonly produces the embryo and endosperm. Monocots and eudicots are nested lineages; the historical label dicots also included other branches and is not one clade.

One embryonic cotyledon defines the familiar name. Parallel veins, three-part flowers and scattered stem bundles are frequent, with exceptions. Palms, grasses, bananas and aloes show why monocots cannot be recognized by growth form alone.

The ancestral pollen pattern has three apertures or derives from it. Two cotyledons are common but also occur outside this clade. Rosids and asterids are major nested branches; their family boundaries rely on multiple traits and molecular evidence.

Living gymnosperms include conifers, cycads, Ginkgo and gnetophytes. Their exposed ovules distinguish them from angiosperms. Cones are common, but neither needle-like leaves nor woody cones characterize every gymnosperm.

Ferns and their relatives are vascular plants without seeds, including horsetails. Sporangia produce spores; fertilization usually needs water for motile sperm. The large leafy plant and the small gametophyte are different stages of one life cycle.

Within Ericales, tea relatives are woody plants with many stamens; heathers often have urn-shaped corollas and specialized anthers; primroses often have five-part flowers. Flower form varies within each family.

Lythraceae commonly have a floral tube surrounding the ovary; Combretaceae often have an inferior ovary and a one-seeded, sometimes winged fruit. Ovary position and fruit structure help distinguish them.
Lauraceae are magnoliids, outside monocots and eudicots. Aromatic tissues and small flowers with anthers opening by valves are useful clues; aromatic leaves alone do not identify this family.

These monocots often have six tepals. Amaryllidaceae commonly bear flowers in an umbel with bracts; Asphodelaceae include aloes but also non-succulent plants; Asparagaceae include very different subfamilies, from lily-of-the-valley to squill relatives. A bulb does not define a family.
Cucurbits commonly combine tendrils, unisexual flowers and an inferior ovary. Their fleshy fruits differ from the pods of legumes: a similar climbing habit does not imply a close relationship.

Rubiaceae often have opposite leaves with stipules between their bases; Apocynaceae commonly have latex and a more specialized reproductive apparatus. Opposite leaves and fused petals occur in both, so several traits must be combined.
Rutaceae often have aromatic oil glands; Sapindaceae include maples, horse-chestnuts and many tropical trees. Maple winged fruits distinguish a genus, not the entire Sapindaceae family.

Solanaceae commonly have fused five-part corollas, five stamens and berries or capsules. Tomato and potato share this family, but different plant organs are eaten; family membership never establishes edibility.
Pines have needles in bundles, while firs and spruces have solitary needles. Woody seed cones and needle attachment help separate genera; a conifer cone is not an angiosperm fruit.

Scale-like leaves are frequent, but junipers can have needle-like leaves. Juniper berry-like structures are fleshy cones, whereas cypress cones are woody. Both differ from the true fruits of flowering plants.
Many members tolerate dry or saline habitats and have paired leaflets. These are ecological and morphological clues, not universal requirements; drought tolerance evolved in many unrelated families.

Lamiaceae often have opposite leaves, two-lipped flowers and four fruitlets; Plantaginaceae include both two-lipped flowers and small plantain spikes. Oleaceae often have two stamens; Pedaliaceae commonly have conspicuous capsules. No single flower shape defines the whole order.

Wind pollination and reduced unisexual flowers are frequent. Fagaceae fruits have a cupule; birch relatives have diverse bracts around fruits; walnut relatives often have pinnate leaves. A hard nut occurs in several families.

Malvaceae often have stellate hairs and mucilage. Hibiscus has an obvious staminal column, but lindens and cacao illustrate other floral arrangements. The family includes more than the familiar mallow flower pattern.

Rosaceae often have showy flowers and many stamens; Moraceae commonly have latex and condensed inflorescences; nettle and elm relatives often have small flowers. Fruit diversity is large: a rose hip, apple and fig do not form in the same way.

Willows have reduced flowers in catkins and small seeds with hairs. Violets have differentiated petals, frequently including a nectar spur. The striking contrast shows why ancestry cannot be inferred from overall appearance alone.

Viburnum relatives often have opposite leaves and small flowers in clusters. Viburnum commonly has drupes whereas elder has berry-like fruits with several stones. Fruit anatomy helps separate these related genera.

Dogwoods commonly have opposite leaves and curved lateral veins. In some species large bracts surround small true flowers. A showy bract and a petal are different organs, even when they perform similar visual roles.
Spindle relatives commonly have small flowers with a nectar disc; some capsules expose seeds surrounded by a fleshy aril. That aril is a seed appendage, different from the fleshy wall of a berry.

Hollies commonly have small flowers and drupes containing several stones. Spiny evergreen leaves are familiar in European holly but are not shared by every species; reproductive traits provide additional clues.

Box relatives commonly have small unisexual flowers and capsules. Evergreen opposite leaves characterize common boxwood but do not define all Buxales. This is an early-diverging eudicot branch, outside the main rosid and asterid groups.

A pod typically develops from one carpel. Pea-like flowers characterize one major legume lineage; mimosoid relatives often have small flowers with conspicuous stamens. Nitrogen-fixing nodules occur in many members, but not all.

In Asteraceae a flower head groups many small flowers on one receptacle. Campanulaceae commonly have a bell-like corolla formed by fused petals. A daisy head is therefore an inflorescence, not one bell-shaped flower.

Buttercup relatives often retain separate carpels and numerous stamens. Poppy relatives commonly have latex and capsules. Both are early-diverging eudicots; petal number and flower symmetry vary substantially within them.
Compound umbels and fruits splitting into two one-seeded parts are common in Apiaceae. Dissected leaves alone are unreliable: similar leaves occur in unrelated plants, including toxic species.

Grasses have small flowers organized in spikelets, often enclosed by specialized bracts. Bromeliads commonly have rosettes and more conspicuous flowers. Their shared monocot ancestry does not make pineapple a grass.

The familiar brassica pattern combines four petals, commonly six stamens and a fruit called a silique or silicle. Some flowers are reduced, so identifying the family requires more than a cross-shaped outline.

Pink relatives commonly have opposite leaves, swollen nodes and capsules. These traits help distinguish them from plants with alternate leaves, but the wider order includes very different cacti and amaranth relatives.

The beak-like fruit divides into five parts. Geranium flowers are commonly radially symmetrical; Pelargonium often has bilateral symmetry. Both belong to Geraniaceae despite being separated into different genera.

Banana pseudostems are formed by overlapping leaf sheaths. Ginger relatives commonly have aromatic rhizomes and flowers with one fertile stamen plus modified sterile stamens. A large herbaceous shoot is not necessarily a woody trunk.

Palms are monocots, often with a crown of large pinnate or fan-shaped leaves. Their trunk thickens differently from an oak trunk. Palm fruits vary: coconut and date illustrate different fruit structures within one family.

Currant relatives are shrubs, commonly with palmately lobed leaves, an inferior ovary and berries. Similar lobed leaves occur in unrelated families; floral organization and fruit help distinguish them.

Allioideae include onion relatives: sulfur compounds often give the characteristic smell, and the ovary is superior. Amaryllidoideae commonly have an inferior ovary. Both are subfamilies within Amaryllidaceae.
Amaryllidoideae include Clivia and many bulbous ornamentals. Their inferior ovary helps distinguish them from the onion subfamily, Allioideae. A bulb is not required: Clivia grows from a rhizome.

Rice belongs to Oryzoideae and the nested tribe Oryzeae. Its spikelets have one fertile flower, commonly six stamens. Wheat and maize belong to other grass lineages; cereal is an agricultural collection, not a taxonomic rank.

Puyoideae contain Puya, largely terrestrial bromeliads with stiff, often spiny leaves. Pineapple belongs to another bromeliad lineage. A water-holding leaf tank or an epiphytic habit is not universal in Bromeliaceae.
Chlorophyta are a green-algal lineage, including unicellular and multicellular forms. They are distinct from Streptophyta, the lineage containing land plants.
Streptophyta include some green algae and all land plants. An alga may therefore be more closely related to a land plant than to another green alga.
Mosses have a dominant leafy gametophyte; the spore capsule remains attached to it. Their leaf-like organs lack the vascular organization of fern or seed-plant leaves.
Liverworts may be leafy or thalloid, with the gametophyte dominant. A flat thallus is therefore not universal; their reproductive structures distinguish them from mosses.

This large angiosperm branch includes monocots, magnoliids and eudicots. Amborella, water lilies and Austrobaileyales are other flowering-plant lineages, outside it. Flowering plants therefore include more than the familiar monocot/eudicot contrast.

Magnoliids include laurels and pepper relatives. They belong to Mesangiospermae alongside monocots and eudicots. Two cotyledons do not make a magnoliid an eudicot: ancestry and pollen characters also matter.

Euphyllophyta unite ferns and seed plants, within vascular plants; lycophytes are another vascular lineage. Broad or divided leaves are common, but leaf size is not the definition and the evolutionary origins of these blades remain debated.

This nested Lamiales branch includes mint relatives and the family of snapdragons and foxgloves. Fused, two-lipped corollas and four stamens in unequal pairs are common, but reductions and reversals occur. Plantains demonstrate that small, nearly radial flowers can also belong here.

This subfamily includes aloes, asphodels and their relatives. Succulent rosettes and toothed margins are familiar in aloes, but other members have softer leaves. Six tepals and six stamens link these contrasting forms; succulence alone does not distinguish their ancestry.

The Prunus lineage includes peaches, apricots, cherries and almonds. Its fruit commonly develops from one carpel with a hardened inner wall, forming a stone. In an almond the edible part is the seed; in a peach the fleshy fruit wall is eaten. This differs from apple and pear pomes.

Apiineae is an infrordinal name retained by the source classification, within Apiales. It must not be confused with the family Apiaceae. Familiar parsley relatives have compound umbels and fruits dividing into two parts, while other Apiales include woody plants with different fruits. Rank and family are separate levels.

This name identifies the chickpea lineage in the archive. Serrated leaflets and papilionaceous flowers help distinguish it from legumes with entire leaflets or small, nearly radial flowers. Some relatives have leaf tendrils, while cultivated chickpea usually has a terminal leaflet. Recent classifications may use Cicerinae within Fabeae.

Oleeae unite olives, ashes and several other olive-family lineages. Fruit structure distinguishes descendants: an olive is a drupe, an ash fruit a samara, and some other members form capsules. Frequently opposite leaves are a shared clue, not proof that all these plants have identical flowers.

The date-palm lineage contains Phoenix. Its pinnate fronds commonly have basal leaflets transformed into spines, and male and female plants are separate. A longitudinally grooved seed helps distinguish it from palms with fan-shaped leaves or different seed anatomy. Date fruits are berries with a membranous inner wall.

Plantain relatives commonly have small four-part flowers, often crowded on leafless flowering axes. Plantago major opens its capsule with a lid; fruit opening varies across the group. These reduced flowers contrast with the large two-lipped flowers of many other Plantaginaceae.

The archive places willows and poplars in this branch. Their unisexual catkins and capsules releasing hairy seeds contrast with other Salicaceae that retain larger floral envelopes or fleshy fruits. The extent of the tribe has varied between classifications; willow characters should not be imposed on every historical member.

This buttercup subfamily includes anemones and pasqueflowers. Many have numerous stamens and separate carpels producing dry fruitlets; their showy floral parts may be sepals rather than petals. Other members produce follicles or have strongly asymmetric flowers, so no one flower outline defines the subfamily.

Agrimony relatives form a nested rosaceous group. In familiar Agrimonia, the floral cup encloses the small dry fruits and bears hooked bristles that aid transport on animals. Those hooks belong to the surrounding cup, not to a peach-like stone. Their prominence varies between relatives.

This rosaceous branch includes agrimony relatives and burnet relatives; Agrimonieae is another name used in classifications. Petals may be conspicuous in agrimony but absent in burnets. Reduced carpels and a persistent floral cup are useful comparisons; these plants need not produce a fleshy rose hip.

Cercidoideae are a legume subfamily including redbud and Bauhinia relatives. Leaves are commonly apparently simple and bilobed, or divided into two leaflets, rather than the many leaflets of a pea leaf. Pea-like flowers can occur here too; that resemblance does not make these plants members of the pea subfamily.

This group includes strawberry relatives and allied rosaceous herbs. In a strawberry, the fleshy receptacle carries many small dry fruits on its surface. Other members have inconspicuous flowers and dry receptacles: a fleshy strawberry-like structure is a feature of some descendants, not a universal requirement.

Kerria and Rhodotypos relatives have few separate carpels, commonly yielding small one-seeded fruits. Petal number varies, and some relatives lack petals. This contrasts with a pear pome or the numerous fruitlets of a strawberry; flower colour alone does not separate these rosaceous lineages.

The archive retains this traditional rubiaceous subfamily name, associated with cinchona relatives and several other lineages. Modern studies have changed its boundaries, and APweb now discusses the broader alliance within Dialypetalanthoideae. Opposite leaves and stipules are often family-level clues; quinine-producing bark is not a universal trait of the group.

Bedstraw and madder relatives often look as though they have whorled leaves: enlarged leaf-like stipules join the true leaves. Their small flowers commonly have four or five lobes. This differs from treating every apparent whorl member as a true leaf, and from the larger woody forms of many other Rubiaceae.

The goji lineage contains Lycium and belongs to Solanaceae. Many members are woody shrubs with small fused corollas, sometimes thorny; berries are common, but fruit anatomy varies. Shrubby habit distinguishes many of them from familiar herbaceous nightshades without defining the whole family.

This cactus subfamily includes many columnar, globose and epiphytic forms. Photosynthetic stems commonly have ribs or tubercles and extremely reduced leaves. Unlike opuntioids, they do not have the characteristic glochids, small barbed bristles. A cactus-like succulent Euphorbia belongs to another family.

Opuntioids commonly have articulated stems and glochids, small barbed bristles carried in areoles. Flattened pads are familiar in Opuntia, but other members have cylindrical segments. These pads are stems; the small true leaves are often short-lived. The contrast with Cactoideae concerns anatomy, not only overall shape.

This palm subtribe includes coconut and Syagrus relatives within Cocoseae. Molecular studies help resolve relationships among these often similar palms. The hard fruit wall with germination pores is a useful comparison within the broader tribe, but a large fibrous coconut is not the fruit shape of every descendant.

These Apiaceae often have simple umbels condensed into head-like clusters, instead of the large compound umbels of parsley relatives. Fruit surfaces commonly bear outgrowths, and floral details vary. Eryngium shows how spiny bracts and a compact flower head can occur inside the umbellifer family.

Horsetails are a fern-related lineage, although they have jointed stems and reduced leaves rather than broad fronds. Their stems perform much of the photosynthesis; spores form in terminal strobili. These spore-bearing structures are not seed cones, and a horsetail produces neither seeds nor true fruits.

Leptosporangiate ferns form their sporangia from a single initial cell. A thin wall and often a specialized annulus help release spores. This contrasts with fern lineages having thicker, differently developing sporangia; frond outline alone cannot identify the subclass.

Only Ginkgo biloba survives today in this lineage, which has a diverse fossil record. Fan-shaped leaves with repeatedly forked veins contrast with typical conifer needles. Its fleshy outer seed coat may resemble a fruit, but there is no enclosing ovary: Ginkgo is a gymnosperm.
